lead: A system held at a fixed temperature cannot turn all of its energy into work: the part TS is tied up with entropy. Subtracting it gives two free energies, the Helmholtz energy A = U − TS and the Gibbs energy G = H − TS. At fixed T and V, −ΔA is the largest total work a change can deliver; at fixed T and P, −ΔG is the largest work other than expansion work, such as electrical work from a cell. Industry uses G for reactors, separators and phase changes at constant pressure, and A for constant-volume and molecular calculations. This chapter defines A and G, derives their differentials and equilibrium tests, and works an ideal-gas compression and the boiling of water.
prereq: You need: internal energy and enthalpy from the first-law chapters, and entropy from the second-law chapters. The full set of four differentials is in fundamental property relations.

blocks.text: A system at temperature T holds internal energy U. Part of U is tied to the random motion counted by entropy S: the product TS. Subtract that part and the remainder is Helmholtz free energy A = U − TS. The same idea at constant pressure starts from enthalpy H = U + PV, so Gibbs free energy G = H − TS = U + PV − TS. Here U is internal energy (J), H is enthalpy (J), T is absolute temperature (K), S is entropy (J/K), P is pressure (Pa), V is volume (m³). A and G carry units of J; per mole they are J/mol.

The subtraction TS removes energy that cannot become work in a reversible isothermal step. A is used when volume is fixed, as in a rigid bomb or a statistical-mechanics lattice. G is used when pressure is fixed, which is the usual laboratory, reactor and pipe condition. Many books write F for the Helmholtz energy; F and A mean the same property. A and G are state functions, because U, H, T and S are, and they are extensive: they double when the amount of material doubles, and for a system of several phases they add up phase by phase.

For a closed system with only pressure-volume work, dU = T dS − P dV. Differentiate A = U − TS: dA = dU − T dS − S dT. Put dU in: dA = −S dT − P dV. Differentiate G = H − TS with dH = T dS + V dP: dG = −S dT + V dP. These are exact differentials for A(T,V) and G(T,P). The variables in brackets are the natural variables: T and V for A, T and P for G.

blocks.where: A is Helmholtz free energy (J); S entropy (J/K); T absolute temperature (K); P pressure (Pa); V volume (m³).
G is Gibbs free energy (J); the other symbols are defined above.

blocks.text: At constant T and V, the second law gives dA ≤ 0 for a spontaneous change in a closed system with only PV work; dA = 0 at equilibrium. At constant T and P, dG ≤ 0, and dG = 0 at equilibrium. The inequality is the practical test: a process at fixed T and P proceeds only if G falls. Work interpretation: at constant T and V, the maximum work obtainable is −ΔA; at constant T and P, the maximum non-PV useful work obtainable is −ΔG.

blocks.where: the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation; G is Gibbs energy (J), H enthalpy (J), T absolute temperature (K).

blocks.text: Derivation: by the quotient rule, [∂(G/T)/∂T]<sub>P</sub> = (1/T)(∂G/∂T)<sub>P</sub> − G/T². From dG, (∂G/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = −S, so the right side is −S/T − G/T² = −(TS + G)/T² = −H/T², because G + TS = H. The equation lets you move a ΔG known at one temperature to another using ΔH alone. For example, a reaction with ΔG = −20.0 kJ and ΔH = −50.0 kJ at 298.15 K, with ΔH taken as constant, has ΔG/T at 350 K = −20 000/298.15 + (−50 000)(1/350 − 1/298.15) = −67.08 + 24.84 = −42.24 J/K, so ΔG(350 K) = −14.8 kJ: still spontaneous, but less so.

sections.h3: Signs and the isothermal ideal-gas result

blocks.text: For an isothermal process on an ideal gas, ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0. Then ΔA = −TΔS and ΔG = −TΔS, so ΔA = ΔG. The entropy change for n moles going from P1 to P2 at constant T is ΔS = nR ln(P1/P2). Therefore ΔA = ΔG = nRT ln(P2/P1). Here n is moles (mol), R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, T is in K, and P1 and P2 are initial and final pressures in the same unit.

Compression has P2 > P1, so ln(P2/P1) > 0 and both ΔA and ΔG are positive. Positive means the surroundings must supply work; the gas does not release it. Expansion gives a negative value. For a real gas or a phase change ΔA and ΔG differ, because ΔU and ΔH are not zero. In general ΔA = ΔU − Δ(TS); only when T is constant does it become ΔU − TΔS, and likewise ΔG = ΔH − TΔS at constant T. At constant T and P a negative ΔG marks a spontaneous phase change or reaction; chemical potential, which extends this to mixtures, belongs to solution thermodynamics.

figure.caption: Left: adding PV turns U into H and A into G, and subtracting TS turns U into A and H into G. Right: the boiling-water example. At the normal boiling point TΔS equals ΔH, so ΔG = 0; ΔU is smaller than ΔH by the expansion work, and ΔA = −PΔV = −3.05 kJ is the only work available.

examples.question: One mole of ideal gas at 300 K is compressed isothermally and reversibly from 1 bar to 5 bar. Calculate ΔA and ΔG. Treat the gas as ideal.
steps: For an ideal gas at constant T, ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0.
The entropy change is ΔS = nR ln(P1/P2) = 1 × 8.314 × ln(1/5) = 8.314 × (−1.6094) = −13.38 J/K.
examples.answer: ΔA = ΔG = +4.01 kJ, so work must be supplied to compress the gas.
examples.check:
import math
n = 1.0
R = 8.314
T = 300.0
P1 = 1.0
P2 = 5.0
dS = n * R * math.log(P1 / P2)
dA = n * R * T * math.log(P2 / P1)
dG = dA
print(round(dA / 1000, 2))
print(round(dG / 1000, 2))

examples.question: One mole of water boils at 1 atm (101.325 kPa) and its normal boiling point, 373.12 K. Steam tables give ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 40.65 kJ/mol and ΔV = V<sub>g</sub> − V<sub>l</sub> = 0.03013 m³/mol. Find ΔS, ΔG, ΔU and ΔA, and say what −ΔA means here.
steps: At the normal boiling point liquid and vapour are in equilibrium at fixed T and P, so the change is reversible: ΔS = ΔH/T = 40 650/373.12 = 108.9 J/K.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = 40 650 − 40 650 = 0, since TΔS = ΔH for this reversible change. Equilibrium at fixed T and P means ΔG = 0.
ΔA = ΔU − TΔS = 37.60 − 40.65 = −3.05 kJ, which equals −PΔV.

Meaning: at constant T the largest total work is −ΔA = 3.05 kJ, and all of it is the expansion work of the steam pushing back the atmosphere. There is no non-expansion work to be had, which is what ΔG = 0 says.
examples.answer: ΔS = 108.9 J/K, ΔG = 0, ΔU = 37.60 kJ, ΔA = −3.05 kJ; the 3.05 kJ is the expansion work of the vapour.
examples.check:
H = 40650.0
T = 373.12
P = 101325.0
dV = 0.03013
dS = H / T
W = P * dV
dU = H - W
dA = dU - T * dS
print(round(dS, 1), round(W), round(dU / 1000, 2), round(dA / 1000, 2))

traps: Writing G = U − TS instead of G = H − TS. Check that G = U + PV − TS; the PV term is missing in the wrong form.
Using Celsius in T. Every free-energy formula uses absolute temperature in kelvin.
Losing the sign for compression. If P2 > P1, ln(P2/P1) is positive, so ΔA and ΔG are positive; expansion gives negative values.
Swapping the equilibrium tests. dA ≤ 0 belongs to constant T,V; dG ≤ 0 belongs to constant T,P.

Forgetting that ΔA = ΔG is special to an ideal gas at constant T. For a real gas or a phase change, at constant T, ΔA = ΔU − TΔS and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS are different numbers; for boiling water at 1 atm, ΔG = 0 but ΔA = −3.05 kJ/mol.
Using ΔA = ΔU − TΔS when the temperature changes. The general form is ΔA = ΔU − Δ(TS) = ΔU − (T₂S₂ − T₁S₁).

quiz.q: Define Helmholtz free energy A and Gibbs free energy G. Give their units.
quiz.a: A = U − TS and G = H − TS = U + PV − TS. Both are in joules (J); per mole they are in J/mol.

quiz.q: Why does subtracting TS turn U or H into a useful work function?
quiz.a: TS is the energy tied to entropy at temperature T. Removing it leaves the part of U or H that can be converted to work in a reversible isothermal process.

quiz.q: Two moles of ideal gas at 400 K expand isothermally and reversibly from 10 bar to 2 bar. Find ΔA and ΔG.
At constant T and P a reaction has ΔG = +2 kJ. Is it spontaneous as written? What if ΔG = −2 kJ?
quiz.a: With ΔG = +2 kJ the reaction is not spontaneous as written; the reverse direction is favoured. With ΔG = −2 kJ the forward reaction is spontaneous.

quiz.q: What does −ΔG represent at constant T and P?
quiz.a: −ΔG is the maximum non-PV useful work obtainable from the process at constant T and P.

quiz.q: Compare the meaning of dA ≤ 0 at constant T,V with dG ≤ 0 at constant T,P.
quiz.a: At constant T,V, a spontaneous closed-system change lowers A; at equilibrium dA = 0. At constant T,P, a spontaneous change lowers G; at equilibrium dG = 0. The fixed variables decide which free energy is the criterion.

quiz.q: A reaction has ΔG = −20.0 kJ and ΔH = −50.0 kJ at 298.15 K. Taking ΔH as constant, use the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation to find ΔG at 350 K.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators use the Gibbs energy to decide phase splits and reaction directions, and fuel-cell designers read the largest electrical work straight from −ΔG. Statistical mechanics links A to the partition function, A = −k<sub>B</sub>T ln Z. Search next for Legendre transforms and the thermodynamic square.
